{{short description|Argentine biologist}}'''Pablo E. Visconti''' is an Argentine professor of [[reproductive biology]] at the  [[University of Massachusetts Amherst]], whose papers on reproduction were recognized as Papers of the Week by both the ''[[Journal of Biological Chemistry]]'' and ''[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]'' in October 2013.<ref name=umass>{{cite news|url=https://www.umass.edu/newsoffice/article/umass-amherst-reproductive-biologists|author=Janet Lathop|title=Reproductive Biologists, with International Team, Move in vitro Fertilization Knowledge Forward|publisher=[[University of Massachusetts Amherst]]|date=October 29, 2013|archive-date=November 7, 2013|access-date=April 17, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131107192852/http://www.umass.edu/newsoffice/article/umass-amherst-reproductive-biologists|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Career==
In 2010, Visconti, Julian Sosnik, and Mariano G. Buffone studied [[CD9]], [[CAPZA3]], and [[IZUMO1]] proteins. During their studies they discovered that CAPZA3 protein was similar to IZUMO1 and is considered to be an inhibitor of [[latrunculin]].<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Julian Sosnik|author2=Mariano G. Buffone|author3=Pablo Visconti|title=Analysis of CAPZA3 localization reveals temporally discrete events during the acrosome reaction|journal=[[Journal of Cellular Physiology]]|volume=224|issue=3|pages=575–580|year=2010|doi=10.1002/jcp.22211|pmid = 20458735|pmc=4058824}}</ref> In 2011 he and his colleagues presented strong evidence of [[transmembrane]] [[adenyl cyclase]] being present in ''[[Rhinella arenarum]]''.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Transmembrane adenylyl cyclase regulates amphibian sperm motility through protein kinase A activation|journal=[[Developmental Biology (journal)|Developmental Biology]]|volume=350|issue=1|year=2011|pages=80–88|doi=10.1016/j.ydbio.2010.11.019|pmid=21126515|pmc=4076105|last1=O'Brien|first1=Emma D.|last2=Krapf|first2=Darío|last3=Cabada|first3=Marcelo O.|last4=Visconti|first4=Pablo E.|last5=Arranz|first5=Silvia E.}}</ref> In 1999, Visconti and his colleagues studied [[sodium bicarbonate]] and suggested that [[cyclic adenosine monophosphate]] in combination with [[tyrosine phosphorylation]] could change [[hamster]] sperm.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Roles of Bicarbonate, cAMP, and Protein Tyrosine Phosphorylation on Capacitation and the Spontaneous Acrosome Reaction of Hamster Sperm|journal=[[Biology of Reproduction]]|volume=61|number=1|year=1999|pages=76–84|doi=10.1095/biolreprod61.1.76|last1=Visconti|first1=Pablo E.|last2=Stewart-Savage|first2=J.|last3=Blasco|first3=Aida|last4=Battaglia|first4=Licia|last5=Miranda|first5=Patricia|last6=Kopf|first6=Gregory S.|last7=Tezón|first7=Jorge G.|pmid=10377034 |doi-access=free}}</ref> In 2013 he and his colleagues from the [[National University of Rosario|Rosario National University]] and the [[National Autonomous University of Mexico]] studied [[in vitro fertilization]] and suggested that pathways in head and tail have different proteins.<ref name=umass/>
